data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible without induction if rationality is redefined as the strategic selection of the most falsifiable survivor to maximize error elimination, but this defense costs the scientist any claim that the preferred theory is more likely to be true or practically reliable in untested domains.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the definition of 'severity' relies on the assumption that future conditions will resemble past conditions, the preference becomes inductive.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If scientists act on corroborated theories because they expect them to work (practical reliability), they are acting inductively regardless of Popper's logical distinctions.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the goal of science is truth rather than just error elimination, preferring a corroborated theory without believing it is closer to truth is irrational.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument reconstructs Popper's 'critical rationalism' by distinguishing between logical probability (which remains zero for universal laws) and methodological preferability. It posits that choosing the best-tested theory is not an inductive inference about the future, but a non-inductive rule of conduct aimed at learning fastest. The mechanism fails if 'severity' of past tests implicitly assumes nature's uniformity, thereby smuggling induction back in as a hidden premise of the testing procedure itself.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
